approach:
# How this course works

A coding agent proposes a change. You decide whether the evidence supports it and whether you can explain it. Every example shows both generation and verification. A test you can rerun is evidence. An agent saying “done” is only a claim, and you check it.

## Twelve teaching weeks, then assessment

The topics and their order follow the public Fall 2026 calendar of Stanford's [CS146S](https://themodernsoftware.dev/), with two verification weeks added. This course is not affiliated with Stanford University. Each teaching week has two 90-minute sessions. The first is a lecture with live generation and verification. The second is a practitioner guest or a studio. When no guest is available, you work on your project or contribution in a studio, with support from the teaching team. Week 13 has the project expo, followed by individual defenses. The [schedule](schedule.en.md) gives topics and deadlines.

## Three lines of work

- **Six assignments:** A1–A6, due in weeks 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 10. Each earns up to 2.5 points (15 total). Keep the artifact, the verification results and a short explanation. End with one decision (accept, narrow, recheck or stop) and the evidence that supports it.
- **Four open-source contributions:** 30 points across two repositories. In the first repository, a small fix earns up to 5 points in week 4, and a substantial change earns up to 10 points in week 8. In the second repository you repeat this: 5 points in week 9 and 10 points in week 12. A TA performs an acceptance review in three cases: the repository has no partner contact, the maintainer has not replied within seven days, or the maintainer declines the contribution as out of scope. Your mark does not depend on a maintainer replying.
- **[A term project](project.en.md):** choose a topic and build runnable software with an agent, alone or with one other student. The four milestones are the proposal, the technical specification, the alpha (one minimal path that runs end to end) and the final version. They earn 2, 4, 6 and 8 points in weeks 2, 4, 7 and 12 (20 total). In a two-person project, the two students share the milestone marks. Each student defends their own understanding separately.

Your term project has its own topic and repository. Attach an AI-use note once to each work item. Then reuse its evidence ID instead of copying logs into several submissions.

## Explain your work without AI

CP1 in week 6 and CP2 in week 11 are thirty-minute checkpoints that you take on paper in class. Each is worth 7.5 points. The week 13 defense is worth 15 points. In a fifteen-minute sitting, without a device, you respond to a change or fault introduced in your own code. Together, these three items provide **30 points of individual evidence without AI**. Participation earns the remaining 5 points through guest questions, studio work and the expo.

Passing requires **at least 60/100 overall, at least 15/30 across CP1, CP2 and the project defense, and at least 5/15 on the defense**. The defense is the only item without AI on your own code, so it has its own minimum mark. Each of those three items allows one resit after feedback if your first mark is below half of the item's maximum. A resit mark that replaces the first mark is capped at half the item's maximum. A sitting can become invalid because of a technical failure or an approved accommodation. You then take an equivalent sitting instead, and it does not use up your resit. Incomplete assessments stay missing. You cannot pass the course while a checkpoint or the defense is missing. Read the [syllabus](../../SYLLABUS.en.md) for the full rules.

## Practise making a decision

Save a prediction before discussion. Inspect a candidate change or a trace. Run a discriminating check, that is, a check that can tell a right result from a wrong one. Revise after feedback, and try a changed input. After checking, choose whether to accept, narrow, recheck or stop. Another generation call helps only when it answers a question you can name.

Follow the safety practices in [Week 0 setup](week0/setup.en.md) before using your supplied coding agent. [Ask for help](staff.en.md) when an access problem or a concept stops you from making progress.

syllabus.markdown:
# Agentic Software Engineering: Build, Verify, Evaluate

English is the first teaching language. By the end of the course you can deliver changes in a real codebase with a coding agent, confirm that the agent got them right, and explain and modify your own work without an agent.

The topics, their order and the position of the deadlines follow the public Fall 2026 calendar of Stanford's [CS146S: The Modern Software Developer](https://themodernsoftware.dev/). This course adds three things: two weeks on verification (weeks 7 and 10); a project defense; and one decision line at the end of every assignment (accept, narrow, recheck or stop), with the evidence behind it. The course is not affiliated with Stanford University. Every assignment, lecture note and rubric here is written for this course.

## Overview

- **Audience and prerequisites**: senior undergraduates and taught master's students in computing or software engineering, with programming, data structures, Git and testing. No experience with AI coding tools is assumed.
- **Length**: 12 teaching weeks, then an assessment week (expo and defenses) in week 13.
- **Two sessions a week**: the first is a lecture that generates work live and then verifies it. The second is a talk by a practitioner guest. In a week without a guest, it is a studio: you work on your own project or contribution while staff circulate. Each session is 90 minutes. The plan is one cohort of 60 students.
- **Three lines of work**: six assignments (mostly in the first six weeks), four open-source contributions (across two repositories), and one term project (one or two people).

## How the course is designed

1. **Verification first**: every example shows both the generating step and the verifying step. No lecture shows "let the agent finish it".
2. **Individual AI-off evidence is a pass condition**: you take the two in-class checkpoints and the defense alone, without AI. Together they carry 30 marks. You do not pass if you score below 15 of those 30 marks, or below 5 of the 15 defense marks.
3. **Marked on engineering evidence**: the project and the contributions are marked on the specification, instruction file, gates, tests, evaluation and your own verification, not on how the interface looks or how many features there are.
4. **Contributions do not depend on luck**: a mark never depends on whether a maintainer replies. Where a repository has no partner contact, a teaching assistant gives an acceptance review.

## Learning outcomes

- **LO1:** Explain a coding agent's loop, system prompt and tool definitions, and predict how it fails on context, tools and stopping.
- **LO2:** Design an agent development workflow: context and specifications, MCP tools, skills, instruction files, hooks, subagents and background tasks.
- **LO3:** Write a requirement as a specification an agent can implement and a test can check, and revise it when new evidence arrives.
- **LO4:** Make an unfamiliar real codebase agent-ready, and deliver a change in it without breaking callers.
- **LO5:** Verify agent-written code with regression and mutation tests, code review, static analysis and security scanning, and defend each acceptance.
- **LO6:** Evaluate agents: check that a test can fail, that the denominator (all the instances a rate is computed over) is complete and that a judge is reliable, and read small-sample results correctly.
- **LO7:** Recognise and mitigate agent security risks (prompt injection, credentials, supply chain), verifying a defense with a local reproduction and a regression.
- **LO8:** Describe how a team operates agents (portals, gateways, routing, cost), and how to recover from an incident and prove the recovery with a regression.
- **LO9:** Collaborate responsibly: follow upstream rules, disclose AI use honestly, submit no low-effort generated work, and decide again when the inputs change.

## Outcomes in teaching and individual assessment

| LO | Teaching introduction | Practice and application | Individual assessment evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| LO1 | Week 1: the internals of coding agents | A1 | CP1; defense |
| LO2 | Weeks 2-4,9: context engineering, skills, customizing the agent and repository, background agents | A2, A3, A4; project | Defense |
| LO3 | Week 2: spec-driven development | Project proposal and technical specification | Defense |
| LO4 | Week 5: agent-ready codebases | A4, A5; contributions | CP1 |
| LO5 | Weeks 6-7: agentic code review and tests that notice a fault | A5; contributions; final project | CP1; CP2 |
| LO6 | Week 10: evaluating agents | A6; final project | Defense |
| LO7 | Week 8: security | Contributions; final project | CP2 |
| LO8 | Week 11: building an AI-native team | Final project | CP2; defense |
| LO9 | Weeks 1-12: every teaching week | The decision line on every assignment; contributions | Defense |

## Calendar

| Week | Topic | First session (lecture) | Second session | Due |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The internals of coding agents | Build a minimal agent live, then read a real agent's requests: system prompt, tool list, loop and stop. | Studio: capture and read your own session. | A1 |
| 2 | Advanced context engineering | Prompting, research–plan–implement workflows and spec-driven development; MCP and tool design for a model reader. | Studio or guest; contribution projects introduced. | A2; project proposal |
| 3 | Agent skills and the CLI | What a skill encodes; trigger tests and near misses; working from the command line. | Guest or studio. | A3 |
| 4 | Customizing your agent and repository | Instruction files, hooks as gates, subagent roles. | Guest or studio. | Contribution 1; project technical specification |
| 5 | Agent-ready codebases | Structure, documentation, tests and checks that let an agent work; scoring readiness. | Guest or studio. | A4 |
| 6 | Agentic code review | What model review catches, misses and invents; disposing of each finding. | CP1 (30 minutes, on paper), then guest or studio. | A5; CP1 |
| 7 | Tests that notice a fault | A surviving mutant is a gap in the tests; a property and its shrunk counterexample; an agent that weakens a test to pass it. | Studio on your project's tests. | Project alpha and task backlog |
| 8 | Security | Text as data or as authority; an inert local injection chain; scan, triage and reproduce. | Guest or studio. | Contribution 2 |
| 9 | Background agents | Asynchronous and parallel agents; issue-to-pull-request pipelines; what changes when nobody is watching. | Guest or studio. | Contribution 3 |
| 10 | Evaluating agents | Can the check fail, was the pass earned, is the denominator complete; pass@k on a small table; calibrating a model judge. | Studio: audit one instance. | A6 |
| 11 | Building an AI-native team | Portals, gateways, routing and cost; recovering from an incident and proving it with a regression. | CP2 (30 minutes, on paper), then guest or studio. | CP2 |
| 12 | The software factory and what comes next | Self-running pipelines as a claim to test; course review. | Defense walkthrough; studio. | Contribution 4; final project |
| 13 | Assessment week | Project expo. | Individual defenses. | — |

Weeks 7 and 10 are this course's additions. The deadline for work due in a week is Sunday 23:59 of that week.

## Assessment

| Component | Marks | When | AI |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Term project: four milestones | 20 | Weeks 2, 4, 7 and 12 | allowed |
| Project defense | 15 | Week 13 | off |
| Four open-source contributions | 30 | Weeks 4, 8, 9 and 12 | allowed |
| Six assignments | 15 | Weeks 1-3, 5, 6 and 10 | allowed |
| CP1: AI-off diagnosis, test and repair | 7.5 | Week 6 | off |
| CP2: AI-off review of unfamiliar code and recovery reasoning | 7.5 | Week 11 | off |
| Participation: guest questions, studio, expo | 5 | All term | — |

To pass, you need all three of these: at least 60/100 overall, at least 15/30 across CP1, CP2 and the defense, and at least 5/15 on the defense. There are no bonus marks. An assessment not yet taken stays missing; it is not scored as zero. You cannot pass the course while a checkpoint or the defense is missing.

CP1, CP2 and the defense each allow one resit. If your first score on one of them is below half of its maximum, you may take one equivalent resit after feedback. The resit has the same learning outcomes, duration and difficulty. Your effective mark is the higher of the two scores. However, when a resit mark replaces the original, it counts for at most half of the item's maximum. The course keeps both the original record and the resit record. You cannot retake a sitting you validly passed to raise your mark. A sitting may be voided by a technical failure or by an approved accommodation. In that case you take an equivalent sitting instead, and it does not use up your resit.

## Assignments

Six assignments are worth 2.5 marks each. For each one, you hand in the work, the verification result and a short explanation. Each one ends with one decision line and the evidence behind it. Note your AI use once. Assignments are marked on completion and evidence. There are no hidden tests.

| Assignment | Week | What you do | LO |
|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | 1 | Capture one real coding-agent session with a forced failure; label each behaviour as observed or inferred. | LO1 |
| A2 | 2 | Build a small MCP tool server; graded on whether a model can pick the right tool, call it correctly and recover. No third-party sign-in is required. | LO2 |
| A3 | 3 | Write one skill for a workflow you first ran by hand; test that it triggers on the right requests and stays quiet on a near miss. | LO2 |
| A4 | 5 | Make a messy repository agent-ready: instruction file, a hook that blocks a bad commit, structure and checks. | LO2, LO4 |
| A5 | 6 | Score a repository's agent readiness with observable anchors and report what would change the score. | LO4, LO5 |
| A6 | 10 | Audit one evaluation instance and its scorer; state what the results do and do not support. | LO6 |

## Term project

You work alone or in a pair, on a topic of your choice. You build working software from scratch with agents. A two-person project has a correspondingly larger scope. The two members of a pair take separate defenses.

| Milestone | Week | Content | Marks |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Proposal | 2 | What it is, who it is for, the core scenario, and the agent's role in development. | 2 |
| Technical specification | 4 | A design document: requirements, key decisions with a rejected alternative each, interfaces and data models, test strategy, what is out of scope. | 4 |
| Alpha and task backlog | 7 | One minimal path that runs end to end; the repository already has an instruction file and one hook gate; a backlog of remaining tasks. | 6 |
| Final | 12 | Working software; tests with their mutation result; one evaluation script; the disposition of a security scan; a README. | 8 |
| Defense | 13 | Fifteen minutes each, no devices: the examiner changes one thing or plants one fault in your own code, and you locate it, explain it and decide what to do. | 15 |

Marks go to engineering evidence only. Any topic is allowed, but a project with an interface and features and no specification, gate, tests or evaluation earns no milestone marks. The two members of a pair share the marks for the proposal, specification, alpha and final. The defense is marked individually. The expo is held in week 13, before the defenses, and counts towards participation.

## Open-source contributions

| Contribution | Week | Repository | Marks |
|---|---|---|---:|
| 1 | 4 | First | 5 |
| 2 | 8 | First | 10 |
| 3 | 9 | Second | 5 |
| 4 | 12 | Second | 10 |

- **Small, then substantial**: the first contribution in each repository is a small onboarding fix (5 marks). The second is a substantive change (10 marks).
- **Two repositories**: you rank your preferences in week 2, and the teaching team assigns your first repository. After contribution 2 you move to a second repository. The point is to learn your way into two different real codebases.
- **Project list**: public open-source projects that partner companies maintain or depend on come first. Other active projects are added after them. A project qualifies if it has an OSI licence, contribution guidelines and an AI-use policy that permits the work, and no CLA (contributor licence agreement) that assigns copyright. At most five students work on one repository at a time. You do not make a marked contribution to a repository owned by your own residency employer. (Your residency employer is the company where you are placed for your residency.) The number of partner repositories and maintainer contacts is not yet confirmed.
- **Completion**: in a repository with a partner contact, a merged pull request meets the completion condition. Sometimes there is no contact, or a maintainer has not replied within seven days. Then a teaching assistant gives an acceptance review instead: the assistant checks the contribution against the project's own contribution guidelines.
- **Quality line**: low-effort AI output scores zero. The maintainer or the teaching assistant decides whether work is low-effort. Each contribution needs a check that fails before the change and passes after it. It also needs your own answers to four questions: what changed, why, which inputs could break it, and what you verified yourself.
- **Boundaries and rights**: contribute to public repositories only. Internal code from your residency, an employer or a partner never enters the course or a model. You may use a pseudonym where the project permits it. You may not want to publish, or to sign a CLA or DCO (Developer Certificate of Origin). Then you may take the course-hosted equivalent route without giving a reason. That route uses the same rubric and has the same maximum mark.

## Workload and participation

There is no hour budget. Weekly time estimates are published after a timed human pilot, a trial run in which people do the work and are timed. The estimates honestly include time spent outside class, and required content is not cut to fit a total.

Each week, the course invites a practitioner to talk about that week's topic in the second session, for at most 45 minutes. A guest makes no product pitch and gives sources for any numbers. Write one question for the guest beforehand. The course runs with however many guests can come. The number is not yet confirmed. Participation marks cover guest questions, studio work and the expo.

## Privacy, fairness and accessibility

Course repositories, prompts, session records and marking material carry no real credentials and no unrelated personal data. Submit only the smallest process record that shows your work, and redact it first. Required materials and activities have keyboard-operable, captioned or text alternatives. You may ask for equivalent time or an equivalent way of taking part. An accommodation keeps the same learning outcomes and the same attainable marks. Oral defenses use a shared rubric and comparable answering time. A second calibrated marker reviews three kinds of case: cases near a threshold, cases where markers disagree, and cases a student asks to have reviewed. Course data is not used for teaching research. Any later use needs ethics approval and your separate consent first.

## Tools and model access

- **Coding agent**: you use a mature coding agent directly. The course states the capabilities it needs (instruction files, hooks, a permission mode, MCP, subagents, a readable session record) and names no vendor.
- **Seats and credit**: every student has a working agent seat or credit when teaching starts, at no cost to the student. The course first uses teaching credit from partners or providers, and its budget buys the rest. How much partners provide is not yet confirmed.
- **Safety**: run the agent in a dedicated directory or container. Keep residency, employer and cloud credentials out of that environment. Keep keys out of repositories, prompts, screenshots and logs. Run the injection demonstration offline, against the local machine only. The [Week 0 setup page](site/docs/week0/setup.en.md) explains each practice and how to check it.
- **Other tools**: pytest, one mutation-testing tool and one property-testing library, Semgrep, gitleaks, pip-audit.

## AI use and responsibility

You do the checkpoints and the defense alone. You may use an agent for all other work, and you note that use once in the work. Nobody infers authorship from writing style. When evidence is contradictory, it goes to a human process.
